questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: What a pair of spectral bands enables
questions.learningObjective: State what two spectral bands enable
questions.stem: On the train dispatcher's log, a scene is captured in two spectral bands. What does that pair primarily enable?
questions.explanation: A pair of bands, one in a numerator-friendly region and one in a denominator-friendly region, enables a normalised difference index. Temperature-only or cloud elimination overstate what bands do.

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: What a normalised difference index measures
questions.stem: A dispatcher asks why a normalised difference index is used instead of a simple band difference. Explain briefly.

answer.exemplar: A normalised difference index divides the difference by the sum, which cancels multiplicative effects such as illumination and sensor gain. A simple difference keeps those scaling effects and varies with brightness.

questions.explanation: Normalising by the sum removes multiplicative scaling, so the index is more comparable across scenes. A raw difference retains illumination variation.

provenance.author: bank-team-human-geography
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: Computing a normalised difference index
questions.stem: On the log, band A reflectance is 0.8 and band B reflectance is 0.2. What is the normalised difference (A-B)/(A+B)?
questions.explanation: (0.8 minus 0.2) divided by (0.8 plus 0.2) equals 0.6 divided by 1.0, which is 0.6. Subtracting only gives 0.6 by coincidence here, but the formula matters.

questions.topic: Registration error in change detection
questions.stem: A dispatcher notices false change along edges in a change-detection map. Explain the likely cause.

answer.exemplar: Misregistration between the two images shifts features by a few pixels, so edges appear to change even when nothing did. The false change follows linear features and boundaries rather than real land-cover change.

questions.explanation: Small spatial offsets make edges look like change. The pattern along boundaries distinguishes registration error from real change.

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: Computing a normalised difference index

stimulus.body: On the log, band P is 0.4 and band Q is 0.6. A dispatcher computes (P-Q)/(P+Q) and gets a negative value. The dispatcher wonders whether the sign is an error.

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: What an unsupervised classification returns
questions.stem: On the log, rerunning an unsupervised classification gives slightly different clusters. Explain why.

answer.exemplar: Unsupervised algorithms start from random initial centres, so different runs converge to slightly different local optima. The overall spectral groupings remain similar, but cluster boundaries and counts can shift.

questions.explanation: Random initialisation leads to different local optima across runs. Results are broadly similar but not identical, so stability checks are wise.

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: Interpreting clusters from a two-band table
questions.stem: On the log, two cluster centres are at (0.2, 0.8) and (0.8, 0.2). What is the Euclidean distance between them?
questions.explanation: Square root of (0.6 squared plus 0.6 squared) equals square root of 0.72, which is about 0.849. Adding the differences gives 1.2, the tempting wrong value.

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: Registration error in change detection
questions.stem: On the log, a dispatcher asks why a 0.5-pixel misregistration matters for 30-metre imagery. Explain briefly.

answer.exemplar: Even half a pixel of misregistration shifts features by 15 metres, creating false change along edges and boundaries. For change detection, that spurious signal can exceed real change in small patches.

questions.explanation: Half a pixel times 30 metres is 15 metres of shift, enough to create false change along edges. The magnitude matters relative to the feature size.

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: What a pair of spectral bands enables
questions.stem: On the log, a dispatcher claims two bands are sufficient for any land-cover study. Which response is most sound?

options.text: Two bands suffice for simple indices but not all covers
Band count does not affect results

questions.explanation: Two bands enable simple indices but cannot separate all covers. More bands help for complex studies, so A is the balanced view.

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: What a normalised difference index measures
questions.stem: Stage 1: An NDI uses NIR and red bands. Stage 2: A pixel has value +0.8. What does this most reliably indicate?

options.text: Strong vegetation signal relative to red

questions.explanation: A high positive NDI indicates vegetation dominates relative to red, not a physical cover fraction or saturation. The value is relative, not absolute.

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: Computing a normalised difference index

stimulus.body: A dispatcher computes (NIR-red)/(NIR+red) and reports 1.2. The NIR value is 0.9 and red is 0.1.

questions.stem: Is the reported value correct?

options.text: No, the correct value is about 0.8

questions.explanation: (0.9 minus 0.1) divided by (0.9 plus 0.1) equals 0.8 divided by 1.0, which is 0.8. The reported 1.2 is an arithmetic error. Indices can approach but not exceed 1 in this form.

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: Registration error in change detection
questions.stem: On the log, a change map shows false change concentrated at field boundaries after a flood event. Explain the most likely cause and remedy.

answer.exemplar: The false change at boundaries indicates misregistration between pre- and post-flood images. The remedy is to coregister the images to sub-pixel accuracy before differencing, then recompute the change map.

questions.explanation: Boundary-concentrated false change is the signature of misregistration. Sub-pixel coregistration before differencing is the standard remedy.
